hint.level_0: A common divisor divides the difference.

So $d\mid (n+1)-n=1$.
The only positive divisor of $1$ is $1$, hence $d=1$.

hint.level_1: Remainders strictly decrease, so it terminates.

In either case the identity holds.

questions.stem: Prove that every multiple of a perfect number (other than the perfect number itself) is abundant ($\sigma(n)>2n$), and that $12$ is the smallest abundant number.
solution_steps: If $P$ is perfect, $\sigma(P)=2P$, i.e. $\sum_{d\mid P}\tfrac1d=2$.
For a multiple $kP$ ($k\ge2$), the divisors include all $kd$ for $d\mid P$, so $\sigma(kP)/(kP)\ge\sum_{d\mid P}\tfrac1d=2$ with strict inequality from extra divisors.
Hence $\sigma(kP)>2kP$: it is abundant.
